CausalChain: Phytochemical binding to MALAT1 triple helix structure -> Induced conformational change in MALAT1 -> Disruption of MALAT1-EZH2 interaction -> Altered recruitment of epigenetic modifiers -> Reprogramming of chromatin states and gene expression in tumor cells -> Increased chemosensitivity
Hypothesis: Plant-derived phytochemicals, when delivered by exosome–liposome hybrid nanoparticles, can target and bind to key structural motifs in oncogenic lncRNAs such as MALAT1. This binding disrupts their interactions with epigenetic regulators, reprogramming tumor chromatin states and gene expression, thereby sensitizing cancer cells to conventional chemotherapy.
Abstract: Recent advances have highlighted the pivotal role of lncRNAs in regulating gene expression in various pathophysiological states, with emerging therapeutic strategies focusing on modulating their structure and interactions. Building on these insights, we propose a novel hypothesis in which plant-derived phytochemicals selectively bind to structured motifs within lncRNAs, such as the triple helix element in MALAT1, thereby inducing conformational changes that disrupt its interaction with epigenetic modifiers like EZH2. This disruption leads to altered chromatin states and reprogramming of gene expression in tumor cells, ultimately sensitizing them to conventional chemotherapeutic agents. Moreover, when delivered via engineered exosome–liposome hybrid nanoparticles, these phytochemical-lncRNA modulators may provide a targeted, low-immunogenicity therapeutic approach. This abstract outlines the mechanistic rationale and therapeutic implications for an innovative combinatorial strategy that targets lncRNA structure to reprogram cancer epigenetics.
